Accuracy ↑
Higher is better

✓
Good for:
Overall correctness on balanced data.

✗
Watch out:

Precision ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
Reliable alerts; fewer false alarms.

✗

Can miss many positives.

Recall ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Finding positives; fewer misses.

✗
Watch out:
Can produce many false alarms.

Specificity ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FP)

✓
Good for:
Correctly clearing negative cases.

✗
Watch out:
Does not show how many positives are caught.

F1 ↑
Higher is better
2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
One score for precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Fβ ↑
Higher is better
(1 + β²) · P · R / (β² · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Choosing emphasis: β > 1 recall, β < 1 precision.

✗
Watch out:
β is not a direct error-cost ratio.

F2 ↑
Higher is better
5 · P · R / (4 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving recall more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check the false-alarm workload.

F0.5 ↑
Higher is better
1.25 · P · R / (0.25 · P + R)

✓
Good for:
Giving precision more emphasis.

✗
Watch out:
Check how many positives are missed.

IMBALANCE
7 metrics
›
Balanced accuracy ↑
Higher is better
(TPR + TNR) / 2

✓
Good for:
Giving both actual classes equal weight.

✗
Watch out:
Equal class weight may not fit your costs.

G-mean ↑
Higher is better
√(TPR · TNR)

✓
Good for:
Requiring both class recalls to be good.

✗
Watch out:
Zero if either class recall is zero.

Youden’s J ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance level
TPR + TNR − 1

✓
Good for:
Choosing a recall–specificity balance.

✗
Watch out:
May not select the lowest-cost cutoff.

MCC ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN − FP · FN) / √((TP + FP)(TP + FN)(TN + FP)(TN + FN))

✓
Good for:
One score using all four outcomes.

✗
Watch out:
Undefined with an empty actual or predicted class.

Cohen’s κ ↑
Higher is better · 0 = chance agreement
(pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ)

✓
Good for:
Agreement beyond expected chance.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with class proportions.

Jaccard / IoU ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Overlap of predicted and true positives.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores correctly predicted negatives.

Markedness ↑
Higher is better
PPV + NPV − 1

✓
Good for:
Trust in positive and negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

ERROR RATES
8 metrics
›
FPR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (FP + TN)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among actual negatives.

✗
Watch out:
Small rates can still mean many alarms.

FNR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (FN + TP)

✓
Good for:
Misses among actual positives.

✗
Watch out:
Says nothing about false alarms.

FDR ↓
Lower is better
FP / (TP + FP)

✓
Good for:
False alarms among positive predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Changes with how common positives are.

FOR ↓
Lower is better
FN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Missed positives among negative predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Can look low when positives are rare.

NPV ↑
Higher is better
TN / (TN + FN)

✓
Good for:
Trust in a negative prediction.

✗
Watch out:
Can look high when positives are rare.

Error rate ↓
Lower is better
(FP + FN) / N

✓
Good for:
Overall share of wrong predictions.

✗
Watch out:
Treats misses and false alarms equally.

Fowlkes–Mallows ↑
Higher is better
√(P · R)

✓
Good for:
Geometric mean of precision and recall.

✗
Watch out:
Ignores true negatives and error costs.

Diagnostic odds ratio ↑
Higher is better
(TP · TN) / (FP · FN)

✓
Good for:
Summarizing test separation as an odds ratio.

✗
Watch out:
Infinite or undefined with zero FP or FN.

RANKING & PROBABILITY
5 metrics
›
ROC-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ TPR d(FPR)

✓
Good for:
Ranking positives above negatives.

✗
Watch out:
High AUC can still mean poor alert precision.

PR-AUC ↑
Higher is better
∫ P dR

✓
Good for:
Precision–recall tradeoffs for rare positives.

✗
Watch out:
Depends on prevalence and integration method.

Average precision ↑
Higher is better
Σₖ (Rₖ − Rₖ₋₁) · Pₖ

✓
Good for:
Precision at successive recall gains.

✗
Watch out:
AP, mAP, and trapezoidal PR-AUC differ.

Log loss ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
−mean(y · ln(p) + (1 − y) · ln(1 − p))

✓
Good for:
Scoring probabilities; penalizing confident errors.

✗
Watch out:
Confident wrong predictions get very large loss.

Brier score ↓
Lower is better · 0 = perfect
mean((p − y)²)

✓
Good for:
Scoring squared probability errors.

✗
Watch out:
Compare with a constant-prevalence baseline.

IN PRACTICE
4 metrics
›
False alarms per hour / km ↓
Lower is better
FP / observed hours or kilometers

✓
Good for:
Estimating alarm burden over time or distance.

✗
Watch out:
Define and group alarm events consistently.

Detection latency ↓
Lower is better
t(detected) − t(event start)

✓
Good for:
Measuring how quickly detection happens.

✗
Watch out:
Report slow cases and missed events too.

Recall lower bound ↑
Higher is better
Lower confidence bound for TP / (TP + FN)

✓
Good for:
Allowing for uncertainty in measured recall.

✗
Watch out:
Needs a stated method and enough test cases.

Recall per scenario ↑
Higher is better
TP / (TP + FN), within each scenario

✓
Good for:
Finding weak spots such as night or rain.

✗
Watch out:
Small groups give uncertain results.

ROC & Trade-offs
A test’s accuracy on sick people is not your chance of being sick.

When you get a Test +, you don’t know whether you came from the sick group or the healthy group. Right now, out of 1,000 people, 500 have the flu (yielding 480 true catches) and 500 are healthy (yielding 20 false alarms). Your actual chance of having the flu is 480 out of all 500 positive tests (96%).

Why a rare disease creates mostly false alarms. When flu is rare (10% sick), 900 of 1,000 people are healthy. A 4% false-alarm rate on 900 healthy people creates 36 false alarms, next to only 96 true catches, so Precision is 72.7%.

With the test cutoff and score separation fixed, changing the sick portion changes Precision while TPR and FPR stay fixed wherever both rates are defined.

Overall Accuracy & The False Security Trap
Why accuracy alone can be dangerously deceptive on rare events
Test Accuracy: (All correct results ÷ Total)
960 out of 1,000 cases correctly classified
96%
Accuracy

Accuracy measures how often the test gives the right answer: catching flu (480 TP) plus clearing healthy people (480 TN).

⚠️ The False Security Trap: When flu is rare (e.g. 10% sick), a broken test that says "Negative" to every single patient achieves an impressive 50% accuracy—while failing to catch a single sick person (TPR = 0%)!

results.text:
Skip to metrics
← CMatrixLab
Quick cheatsheet →
Print / PDF
Metrics reference

What does each score tell you? Explore simple explanations and examples from medicine, driving, fraud detection, and more.

Help me choose a metric

Choose by the decision you need to make: finding problems, reducing false alarms, keeping a review queue manageable, or trusting a predicted chance.

You do not want to miss a problem

Use recall to see how many real problems you catch. FNR tells you how many you miss.

Examples: finding an illness in a medical test, or spotting a pedestrian in front of a car. Check false alarms too, and test situations such as night or rain separately. Medical example · AEB example

You want fewer false alarms

Use precision to check how many alerts are real. FPR tells you how often normal cases get flagged.

Examples: keeping legitimate emails out of spam, avoiding wrong fraud blocks, or reducing unnecessary car warnings. Check that you still catch enough real problems. Automatic-blocking example

You want one overall score

Use accuracy for a simple count of correct predictions. If one class is much rarer, also check balanced accuracy or MCC.

Example: finding faulty parts in a factory where almost every part is good. Always look at missed defects and rejected good parts separately. Factory example

You want the most likely problems first

Use ROC-AUC to check the ordering of scores. For rare problems, PR-AUC or AP also helps show how useful the alerts are as you find more cases.

Example: putting suspicious payments at the top of a fraud review queue. Check the results for the number of payments your team can actually review. Review-queue example · Object-detection example

You need to trust the predicted chances

Use log loss or Brier score to check probability predictions.

Example: if many patients each receive a 20% risk estimate, does about 1 in 5 have the condition? A calibration plot helps you check this. Risk-score example

You care about what happens over time

Check false alarms per hour or kilometer, detection delay, and track recall.

Example: a car should spot a pedestrian quickly, keep following them, and avoid repeated false warnings. Decide what counts as one warning before measuring it. Driving-hours example · Rare-hazard example

Choose the setting that catches enough problems without causing too many false alarms. Try a scenario in the calculator ↓
